Battle of Gaugamela. Near the village of Gaugamela in northern Mesopotamia in 331 BC, Alexander the Great faced the Persian King Darius III in the definitive clash between their empires. Alexander's cavalry tactics and discipline shattered the Persian army and effectively ended the Achaemenid Empire.

Alexander commanded approximately 47,000 Macedonian troops, vastly outnumbered by what may have been 100,000 or more Persian soldiers plus war elephants. Darius positioned his army on open ground, hoping to maximize his numerical advantage. He deployed elephants and scythed chariots, weapons designed to terrify soldiers unfamiliar with them.

But Darius had misunderstood his opponent. Alexander's cavalry, led by the elite Companion Cavalry, executed a devastating oblique attack. Rather than meet the Persians head-on, Alexander targeted Darius himself and his personal guard. The Persian center collapsed in panic when Darius fled the field.

Disciplined Macedonian phalanxes then finished the rout, overwhelming Persian formations that were already breaking. Darius escaped from the immediate battle but was killed months later in flight, ending any effective Persian resistance.

The victory ended the Achaemenid Dynasty entirely. Alexander's Macedonian Empire became the undisputed superpower of the known world. With Gaugamela, Alexander achieved the apex of his dominance and his legendary status. Darius III, whose empire seemed invincible, could not withstand Macedonian innovation and the genius of its young commander.

Alexander had previously defeated Darius at Issus, but Gaugamela was the decisive blow that shattered Persian power forever. The battle was the climax of the broader Macedonian conquest, the campaign that remade the entire eastern world under Alexander's rule.
